content: The accuracy of diagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB) drug resistance was evaluated using a multivariable, mixed-effects model. All drugs were downgraded by one level for indirectness in sensitivity and specificity due to the enrichment of studies for rifampicin resistance, which raised concerns about their applicability. Additionally, specificity for rifampicin, levofloxacin, and pyrazinamide was further downgraded for imprecision, while ethambutol was downgraded for risk of bias because different samples were used for the index and reference tests. The overall certainty of evidence for test accuracy ranged from moderate to very low. The diagnostic performance of the tests was found to be accurate for all drugs assessed. The pooled sensitivity was at least 95% for isoniazid, moxifloxacin, and ethambutol; over 93% for rifampicin and levofloxacin; and 88% for pyrazinamide. The pooled specificity was at least 96% for all drugs. The reference standard for isoniazid, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin was culture-based phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST), while a combination of phenotypic DST and whole genome sequencing (WGS) was used for rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. The percentage of tests with indeterminate results ranged from 9% (levofloxacin and moxifloxacin) to 18% (pyrazinamide), with higher indeterminate rates observed in samples with lower bacterial loads. For some drugs, the overall certainty of evidence was high. However, levofloxacin was downgraded for inconsistency, while bedaquiline and linezolid were downgraded by two levels for imprecision due to a low number of resistant samples and wide confidence intervals. Clofazimine was also downgraded by two levels—one for inconsistency (due to outlier studies) and another for imprecision. Amikacin was downgraded for sensitivity and specificity because critical concentrations outside WHO recommendations were used in many samples. Its sensitivity was further downgraded for inconsistency and imprecision. Ethambutol was downgraded for risk of bias due to the use of different samples for index and reference tests, while streptomycin specificity was downgraded for inconsistency and imprecision. Among individuals with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), the tests were highly accurate for isoniazid, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ethambutol, and streptomycin (pooled sensitivity ≥95%) and acceptable for pyrazinamide (90%), bedaquiline (68%), linezolid (69%), clofazimine (70%), and amikacin (87%). The pooled specificity was 95% or greater for all drugs except streptomycin (75%). The reference standard for all drugs was phenotypic DST, except for ethambutol and pyrazinamide, where a combination of phenotypic DST and WGS was used. Indeterminate test results ranged from 9% (levofloxacin and moxifloxacin) to 21% (ethambutol), with higher rates in samples with low bacterial loads. The cost-effectiveness of targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) for diagnosing drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) was assessed through a systematic review and modeling analysis. The cost of targeted NGS was estimated to range from $134 to $257 in South Africa, $120 to $198 in Georgia, and $121 to $175 in India. The analysis showed that targeted NGS was cost-effective in South Africa but not in Georgia. In India, targeted NGS was more cost-effective than the current DST practices, with lower costs and greater health gains. Implementation of targeted NGS faces several challenges, including high technical complexity, the need for specialized laboratory infrastructure, and supply chain issues. The technology requires uninterrupted electricity, high internet connectivity, and advanced data management systems. While targeted NGS is seen as a significant advancement in molecular diagnostics for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), its high cost and technical demands may limit its feasibility in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Stakeholders expressed concerns about the affordability and equity of access to targeted NGS, particularly in centralized laboratory settings. The technology may not be suitable for decentralized use, which could limit access in regions without reference laboratories. Participants emphasized the need for targeted NGS to balance accuracy, speed, affordability, and equity before widespread implementation in LMICs.
